insights.title: Why enterprise AI agents fail after the POC
insights.one_liner: A production agent needs a controlled execution environment around the model, not just a model connected to tools.
insights.why_this_matters: Many agent demos prove task capability but do not prove that the surrounding system can authorize, observe, interrupt, reconstruct and evaluate real work.

whole_source_map.problem: POC architecture often omits controls and state-management properties required in production.
whole_source_map.thesis: Enterprise agent architecture should be designed around controlled execution rather than model calls alone.
core_topics: separation of orchestration and protected data

derived_model.problem: A model can complete a task without the organization being able to govern the task.
derived_model.mechanism: Put identity, authority, durable history, protected data access, human intervention and replay around execution.
derived_model.result: The same work becomes more controllable, explainable and testable regardless of whether the executor is an AI model or a person.

central_chain: A proof of concept demonstrates that a model can perform a task.
Production use turns that task into consequential organizational work that requires authority, state, evidence and recovery.
Execution history, protected data access, executor-independent tasks and replay form one control layer around the model.
That layer makes the work more explainable, interruptible and testable over time.
open_gaps: The talk establishes architectural primitives more strongly than concrete implementation guidance; adjacent tools are therefore project-added learning connections.
The YouTube upload date is not independently verified.

examples.scenario: An agent is allowed to update a customer record or execute another consequential business action.
examples.question: Can the system later reconstruct the request, authority, context, policy, executor, action and verification?
Can the system explain months later why a customer was changed, under whose authority, using which context and approval?

limitations: An append-only history still needs identity evidence, policy and component versions, retention, tamper protection and meaningful event semantics.
Separating data and orchestration reduces exposure but does not automatically eliminate prompt injection or data exfiltration.
Human handoff still requires ownership, locking, idempotency, approval authority, timeout and recovery rules.
Replay is only useful when reconstructed context and evaluation criteria are trustworthy.

use_now: Evaluate agent architectures by asking whether consequential work can be reconstructed and explained later.
try: Model one real workflow as an executor-independent task with explicit authority and verification.
Experiment with a small policy-as-code rule using Open Policy Agent.
build: A minimal execution-ledger prototype for an agent workflow.
watch: How production agent platforms standardize identity, policy, handoff and replay.

insights.title: Temporal: the mental model behind durable execution
insights.one_liner: Temporal moves workflow progress out of one process and into durable execution state so Workers can fail, restart and continue the work.
insights.why_this_matters: Retries are easy to describe and surprisingly hard to compose across multi-step, long-running work. Temporal is useful to understand because it changes the unit of reliability from a running process to a persisted Workflow Execution.

whole_source_map.problem: Long-running or multi-step processes become fragile when their progress exists mainly inside one process and every failure path must be rebuilt manually.
whole_source_map.thesis: Temporal provides durable execution by persisting Workflow Execution state and progress in the Temporal Service while Worker Processes execute tasks from queues.

derived_model.problem: If process progress lives only in application memory, a crash can turn recovery into custom state-management code.
derived_model.mechanism: Temporal keeps Workflow Execution progress as persisted Event History; Workers poll tasks, execute Workflow/Activity code, record progress, and can later reconstruct workflow state from history.
derived_model.result: The process can survive Worker or process failures and continue from durable state instead of treating every restart as a new workflow.

central_chain: A multi-step process needs state that outlives the process currently executing it.
Temporal represents the process as a Workflow Execution whose progress is persisted by the Temporal Service as Event History.
Worker Processes poll Task Queues and execute Workflow or Activity work, so Workers are replaceable executors rather than the sole owners of workflow state.
Retry Policies and timeouts help repeat failed work, while external effects still need safe/idempotent Activity design.
The useful outcome is durable continuation across failures, waits and long-running work.
open_gaps: Exact replay/determinism coding constraints differ by SDK and should be checked in the chosen language guide before implementation.
Advanced history management, production topology and Temporal Cloud operations are intentionally outside this first mental model.

nodes.label: 01 · Start
nodes.title: Workflow Execution
nodes.text: A client starts durable work whose identity and progress live beyond one Worker process.

nodes.label: 02 · Persist
nodes.title: Event History
nodes.text: The Temporal Service records Events in an append-only history representing Workflow Execution state.

nodes.label: 03 · Dispatch
nodes.title: Task Queue
nodes.text: Workflow and Activity tasks are made available for Worker Processes to poll and execute.

nodes.label: 04 · Execute
nodes.title: Worker + Activity
nodes.text: Workers run application code; side-effecting work can retry and therefore needs safe external-operation semantics.

nodes.label: 05 · Recover
nodes.title: Replay and continue
nodes.text: If a Worker disappears, persisted history remains and workflow state can be reconstructed so execution continues.

image.reason: The important idea is the movement and persistence of workflow state; a sequence/layer diagram teaches this more precisely than a generated illustration.

concepts.name: Workflow Execution
concepts.why_needed: This is the durable unit of execution; it is not equivalent to one running Worker process.

concepts.name: Event History
concepts.why_needed: Temporal defines it as an append-only log of Events representing the full state of a Workflow Execution.

concepts.name: Worker Process + Task Queue
concepts.why_needed: Workers poll queues and execute code, which separates durable workflow state from any single executor process.

concepts.name: Activity Execution
concepts.why_needed: Activities are the practical boundary for work that interacts with external systems and can be retried.

concepts.name: Idempotency under retry
concepts.why_needed: A retry can repeat external work; Temporal's documentation explicitly calls for idempotent Activity design to avoid duplicate effects.

examples.scenario: A multi-step onboarding process waits for external APIs, human input and later retries.
examples.question: Should progress survive process restarts without writing custom recovery tables and retry orchestration for every step?

examples.scenario: An agent workflow invokes tools over minutes or hours and may wait for approval or external results.
examples.question: Is the agent loop important enough that a Worker restart should not erase which steps already completed or what should happen next?

limitations: Temporal introduces a workflow runtime, SDK programming model and service dependency; simple stateless request-response or short best-effort jobs may be better served by lighter infrastructure.
Retries do not make external effects exactly-once. Activities that can be retried still need idempotent or otherwise safe interactions with external systems.
Workflow logic must respect Temporal's replay/execution model; arbitrary non-deterministic behavior cannot be treated like ordinary in-process code.
This explainer deliberately stops before advanced history lifecycle, deployment versioning, replication, scaling and Cloud operations.

use_now: Use the durability question when designing any long-running automation: where does progress live if the current process disappears?
try: Install Temporal CLI and run the official local development service with `temporal server start-dev`.
Run one official language quickstart, then restart the Worker during a deliberately multi-step workflow and inspect what persisted in the Web UI/Event History.
learn: Retry Policy, timeouts and Activity idempotency
build: A tiny long-running agent or approval workflow where an external/tool call is an Activity and workflow progress survives a Worker restart.
watch: Whether durable workflow runtimes become a common substrate for production AI-agent execution rather than each agent framework rebuilding recovery semantics.
ignore_for_now: Temporal Cloud, multi-region replication, Nexus and advanced production tuning until the local durable-execution model proves useful.
